title: How do you manage test data (JSON/CSV fixtures, DB seeding, API-generated data, environment config, factory methods, randomized/synthetic data), and how do you keep parallel tests from interfering (isolated data per worker, unique keys, independent setup/teardown)?
shortTitle: Managing test data and keeping parallel tests from interfering
keyPoints: Test data comes from multiple sources: static fixtures, DB seeding, API generation, config, factories, and synthetic randomization
API-generated data is often best because it goes through real validation, stays consistent with business rules, and returns real IDs
Factory methods build valid objects with sensible defaults and selective overrides, reducing duplication and clarifying intent
Parallel interference happens when concurrent tests read and write the same data, producing flaky order-dependent failures
Isolate data per worker using unique keys built from random values, UUIDs, or the worker index so tests never collide
Each test should create its own data and clean up independently, never relying on state left by another test

s1_definition.oneliner: Supply test data through fixtures, DB seeding, API generation, config, factories, and synthetic randomization, and keep parallel tests independent by isolating data per worker, using unique keys, and giving each test its own setup and teardown.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Static fixtures** – JSON or CSV files with stable, versioned reference data. Simple but shared and can go stale.
- **DB seeding** – Insert known rows directly. Fast for complex relational preconditions but must avoid parallel collisions.
- **API-generated data** – Create preconditions through the app's own endpoints. Best: goes through real validation, returns real IDs.
- **Factory methods** – Build valid objects programmatically with defaults and selective overrides.
- **Synthetic data** – Generate realistic fake values for uniqueness and coverage.
- **Parallel isolation** – Per-worker or per-test data with unique keys, independent setup and teardown.
s1_definition.analogy: When many testers at the National Bank of India run checks at the same time, each needs their own sample customers and accounts, or they will step on each other. Good test-data management gives every tester their own set of practice accounts with unique numbers, and each tester tidies up afterward so the next run starts clean.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Test Data Sources
  ─────────────────

  ┌───────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐  ┌───────────────┐
  │ Static Fixture │  │ API Generated │  │ Factory Method│
  │ JSON/CSV       │  │ POST /api/... │  │ create(opts)  │
  │ Versioned      │  │ Real validation│ │ Defaults +    │
  │ Read-only      │  │ Returns real ID│ │ overrides     │
  └───────────────┘  └───────────────┘  └───────────────┘

  Parallel Isolation
  ──────────────────

  Worker 1         Worker 2         Worker 3
  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐
  │ACC-W1-001  │  │ACC-W2-001  │  │ACC-W3-001  │
  │ACC-W1-002  │  │ACC-W2-002  │  │ACC-W3-002  │
  │  (unique)  │  │  (unique)  │  │  (unique)  │
  └────────────┘  └────────────┘  └────────────┘
       │               │               │
       └───────────────┴───────────────┘
                  No overlap
                  No interference
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
I manage test data from multiple sources chosen by the situation: static fixtures for versioned reference data, API generation for preconditions that go through real validation, factory methods for objects with sensible defaults, and synthetic data for uniqueness. The harder half is keeping parallel tests from interfering: I isolate data per worker with unique keys, give each test independent setup and teardown, and never hard-code a shared mutable record.

The core principle is that every record a test creates carries a unique identifier, built from a UUID, timestamp, or worker index, so parallel tests never collide. Each test creates exactly the data it needs and cleans up afterward, making it self-contained and runnable in any order.

At the National Bank of India our regression ran across many parallel workers, and early on we had flaky failures because transfer tests shared a fixed account. I fixed it by generating uniquely keyed accounts per test through the API and giving each test its own setup and teardown. The flakiness disappeared.

Remember one sentence: isolate test data per worker with unique keys and independent setup and teardown so parallel tests never share mutable state.
